questions.q: Why does 'SELECT ... FROM Products WHERE ROWNUM <= 10 ORDER BY ListPrice DESC' fail to return the 10 most expensive products on Oracle?
options: ROWNUM is assigned before ORDER BY runs, so it numbers unsorted rows and filters them before sorting happens
Oracle doesn't support ROWNUM at all
ORDER BY is illegal in the same query as WHERE on Oracle
ROWNUM can only be used with INSERT statements
questions.explain: ROWNUM numbers rows as the table scan produces them, and the WHERE filter runs before the ORDER BY sort — so you get 10 arbitrary rows, then sorted, not the top 10 by price.

questions.q: What's the correct traditional (pre-12c) Oracle pattern to get the 10 most expensive products?
options: Sort the data inside a subquery first, then apply WHERE ROWNUM <= 10 to the already-sorted result
Apply WHERE ROWNUM <= 10 directly, then sort the 10 rows afterward
Use TOP (10) like SQL Server
ROWNUM cannot be fixed; it only works on unsorted data
questions.explain: Wrapping the sorted query in a subquery means ROWNUM is applied to rows that are already in the correct order.

questions.q: Which clause does SQL Server's TOP lack that forces you to use OFFSET/FETCH for true pagination (e.g. 'page 2')?
options: The ability to skip a number of rows before returning results
The ability to limit how many rows come back
The ability to use ORDER BY at all
The ability to use TOP with a WHERE clause
questions.explain: TOP only limits row count; it has no built-in concept of skipping rows, which OFFSET provides.

questions.q: What pagination syntax do MySQL and PostgreSQL share natively?
options: LIMIT ... OFFSET ...
ROWNUM <= ...
FETCH FIRST ... ONLY (exclusively, with no LIMIT support)
questions.explain: Both MySQL and PostgreSQL support LIMIT n OFFSET m as their native pagination clause; PostgreSQL additionally accepts the ANSI OFFSET/FETCH form.

questions.q: Which of these platforms support the ANSI-standard OFFSET n ROWS FETCH NEXT m ROWS ONLY syntax?
options: SQL Server (2012+), Oracle (12c+), and PostgreSQL
Only SQL Server
Only Oracle
None of them — it's a theoretical standard with no real implementations
questions.explain: SQL Server 2012+, Oracle 12c+, and PostgreSQL all implement the ANSI SQL:2008 OFFSET/FETCH syntax, even though MySQL and older Oracle versions do not.
